```{r}
#| include: false
# scripts/render_docs.sh copies tests/fixtures/tiny into SCX_DOCS_WORK, so
# the code below can name the files directly. Python cells come from
# _convert-py.qmd, rendered by Jupyter in its own process.
work <- Sys.getenv("SCX_DOCS_WORK")
if (!nzchar(work)) stop("SCX_DOCS_WORK is not set: render with scripts/render_docs.sh")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = work)
```

This page takes one small H5Seurat file, looks inside it, converts it to
AnnData `.h5ad`, and checks the result. Each step is shown three ways: with
the `scx` command line, with the Python package and with the R package. All
three call the same engine, so they detect the same formats and use the same
defaults.

The example file, `tiny_v4.h5seurat`, is a 6-cell by 5-gene dataset from the
SCX test fixtures. The second cell has no counts and two genes are each
expressed in a single cell, so empty cells and sparse genes are part of the
example.

## Look before converting

`inspect` reads only metadata: the format, the shape, the column names and
the embedding keys. The count matrix is not loaded, whatever the file size.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## CLI

```{bash}
scx inspect tiny_v4.h5seurat
```

## Python

{{< embed _convert-py.qmd#py-inspect echo=true >}}

## R

```{r}
library(picklerick)

info <- inspect("tiny_v4.h5seurat")
info[c("format", "n_obs", "n_vars", "obs_cols")]
```

:::

## Convert

The input format is detected from the file's content; the output format is
chosen by the extension of the output path. The matrix is streamed in chunks
of 5000 cells by default, so peak memory does not grow with the number of
cells.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## CLI

```{bash}
scx convert tiny_v4.h5seurat tiny_cli.h5ad
```

## Python

{{< embed _convert-py.qmd#py-convert echo=true >}}

## R

```{r}
convert("tiny_v4.h5seurat", "tiny_r.h5ad")
```

:::

## Check the result

The converted file has the same shape and cell metadata as the source.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## CLI

```{bash}
scx inspect tiny_cli.h5ad
```

## Python

{{< embed _convert-py.qmd#py-check echo=true >}}

## R

```{r}
sce <- read_h5ad("tiny_r.h5ad")
sce
```

:::

## Convert a subset of cells

`--where` writes only the cells whose `obs` matches, without reading the
whole file into memory first: the matrix still streams in chunks. Give it
`column=value`; repeat it to accept more values of a column (they OR
together) or to filter on more columns (they AND together). Values are
compared as text, booleans as `True`/`False`, and missing values never
match. Python and R take the same filter as a dict or a named list.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## CLI

```{bash}
scx convert tiny_v4.h5seurat tcells_cli.h5ad --where cell_type=T
scx inspect tcells_cli.h5ad
```

## Python

{{< embed _convert-py.qmd#py-where echo=true >}}

## R

```{r}
"tiny_v4.h5seurat" |> convert("tcells_r.h5ad", where = list(cell_type = "T"))
colnames(read_h5ad("tcells_r.h5ad"))
```

:::

The output holds the matching cells in X, every layer, raw counts, `obs`
and `obsm`. Cell-by-cell graphs in `obsp` keep only the rows and columns of
those cells, renumbered. Genes (`var`, `varm`) and `uns` are copied
unchanged. A filter that matches nothing writes a valid file with no cells;
a column that `obs` doesn't have is an error that lists the columns it has.

On `.h5ad`, Zarr, dgCMatrix H5Seurat and 10x HDF5 input only the matching
cells of the matrix are read. BPCells and MatrixMarket input can't read a
range of cells on its own, so it is read through and the other cells are
dropped as they pass: the same output, at the cost of a full read. The
values follow the shell's quoting rules, so quote one that has spaces:
`--where "cell_type=CD4 T"`. Everything up to the first `=` is the column
name.

## Provenance

`scx convert` records where its output came from, in two places. The
`provenance` section of `scx inspect tiny_cli.h5ad` above is the first: a
block in `uns["scx_provenance"]` with the SCX version and the source file's
path and SHA-256. It depends only on the input, so it is the same every
time that input is converted.

The second is a sidecar file next to the output, which adds what is
particular to one run: when the conversion ran, and the output's SHA-256 and
shape.

```{bash}
cat tiny_cli.h5ad.prov.json
```

A conversion with `--where` adds the filter to both records, as
`"where": {"cell_type": ["T"]}`.

In a pipeline that downloads its input, `--source-url` adds the origin URL
to both records, and `--source-sha256` passes in a hash the downloader
already computed, so SCX doesn't read the source a second time to hash it.

Provenance is written by the command line only: `convert()` in Python and R
writes neither the block nor the sidecar. The record formats are described
in [docs/provenance.md](https://github.com/btraven00/scx/blob/main/docs/provenance.md).

## Options shared by all three

| Option | CLI | Python | R | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cells per streamed chunk | `--chunk-size` | `chunk_size=` | `chunk_size =` | 5000 |
| Output matrix type | `--dtype` | `dtype=` | `dtype =` | `f32` |
| Seurat assay (H5Seurat input) or MuData modality (`.h5mu`) to read | `--assay` | `assay=` | `assay =` | `RNA`; for `.h5mu` the only modality, else `rna` |
| Seurat layer to read (H5Seurat input) | `--layer` | `layer=` | `layer =` | `counts` |
| Keep only matching cells | `--where col=value` | `where={"col": v}` | `where = list(col = v)` | every cell |

The full lists are in each reference: `scx convert --help`,
`picklerick.convert` and `?picklerick::convert`.
